questionText: What is deferred execution, and which operators trigger immediate execution?
shortAnswer: Deferred operators (Where/Select/OrderBy/Join/GroupBy) build a query that runs on enumeration; immediate operators (ToList/Count/First/Sum/Average/Aggregate) execute now. Consequences: exceptions surface late, re-enumeration re-runs everything, and mutating the source between runs changes results.
detailedAnswer: Deferred pipeline: var q = source.Where(...).Select(...) — zero work until foreach/ToList/enumeration; each enumeration re-executes from scratch (two ToLists = two full passes, two DB queries for IQueryable!). Immediate: ToList/ToArray/ToDictionary/ToLookup/ToHashSet (materialize), Count/Any/First/Single/Aggregate/Sum (scalar — must consume to answer). Implications: (1) Errors (null source, bad predicate) throw at enumeration, not construction — validate inputs eagerly outside the query. (2) Source mutation between enumerations changes results (or throws version exceptions) — snapshot with ToList when the source may move. (3) Logging/debugging inside predicates runs per enumeration (confusing counts — materialize once, then inspect). (4) Returning IEnumerable<T> from methods/APIs leaks deferred work + source lifetime (disposed DbContext on later enumeration — the classic ObjectDisposedException; repositories must ToList before returning). Rule: defer inside a method, materialize at boundaries (return ToList, never the query). OrderBy is deferred but buffers fully on first MoveNext (sort needs everything) — deferred ≠ streaming.
internalWorking: Deferred operators return iterator state machines (compiler-generated, holding source + delegates); MoveNext pulls through the chain. Immediate operators loop to completion (ToList grows a buffer; scalars fold). IQueryable defers further: expression tree built now, translated + executed by the provider on enumeration.
realWorldUsage: Repository returns (ToList before dispose), API shaping pipelines, lazy report builders, and test assertions (materialize once, assert many).
commonMistake: Returning IEnumerable from a using-scoped context (disposed on enumerate), enumerating twice expecting caching (re-runs — ToList once), and debugging predicates with side effects (counts that change per inspection).
technicalConversation: Ask where their repositories materialize — ToList inside the method (correct) versus returning IQueryable/IEnumerable queries (leaks lifetime + intent).
interviewFollowUp: Why does OrderBy defer yet still need the whole sequence before yielding the first item?
keyTakeaway: Deferred builds, immediate runs. Materialize at trust, lifetime, and API boundaries.

questionText: Which LINQ operators stream and which buffer, and why does it matter?
shortAnswer: Streaming (Where/Select/Take/Skip/Zip/Concat) yields item-by-item with O(1) memory; buffering (OrderBy/GroupBy/Reverse/Distinct/Join/ToList) must consume input before yielding. It matters for infinite streams, huge datasets, latency-to-first-result, and memory ceilings.
detailedAnswer: Streaming pipeline: source.Where(f).Select(g).Take(10) touches only what Take demands (pull-based — infinite sources OK, first result immediate). Buffering breaks streaming: OrderBy sorts everything before yielding row one (O(n) memory + full latency); GroupBy/Join/Distinct build tables; Reverse buffers (except on indexable fast paths); ToList/ToArray/ToDictionary materialize by contract. Design consequences: (1) Put buffering as late as possible (filter/project first — less to buffer). (2) Infinite/streaming sources tolerate only streaming ops (sensor feeds, log tails, IAsyncEnumerable pipelines). (3) First-result latency: streaming UIs render progressively; a misplaced OrderBy stalls everything. (4) Memory: buffering a 10M-row set needs the whole set resident — Chunk/stream instead. (5) EF: streaming vs buffering maps to server cursors vs tempdb sorts — same reasoning, bigger numbers. Custom operators: implement streaming with yield (document when yours buffers — e.g. a Median operator must). Testing: infinite test sequences (Enumerable.Repeat + Take) prove streaming; memory assertions prove non-buffering.
internalWorking: Streaming iterators chain MoveNext calls (each pull descends the pipeline — no storage). Buffering operators allocate tables/arrays on first MoveNext and drain input before yielding (OrderBy: key array + sort; GroupBy: lookup; Distinct: set). Take(n) short-circuits upstream disposal after n items.
realWorldUsage: Log tailing, sensor pipelines, progressive UI rendering, ETL transforms, and infinite test data.
commonMistake: OrderBy before Take on streams (stalls forever on infinite input), buffering huge sets (OOM), and assuming Take(10) makes OrderBy cheap (sort still processes everything).
technicalConversation: Ask for their time-to-first-result on the biggest pipeline — a buffering operator early in the chain is usually the answer.
interviewFollowUp: How would you prove a custom operator streams, using only public API behavior?
keyTakeaway: Stream by default; buffer deliberately and late. Infinite input tolerates streaming ops only.

questionText: What is the difference between IEnumerable<T> and IQueryable<T>, and what are expression trees?
shortAnswer: IEnumerable<T> holds compiled delegates executed in memory; IQueryable<T> holds an expression tree + provider that translates it (to SQL) and executes remotely. Same LINQ surface, radically different execution: memory loops versus translated queries.
detailedAnswer: IEnumerable.Where takes Func<T,bool> (IL — runs as code). IQueryable.Where takes Expression<Func<T,bool>> (data describing code — the provider walks the tree emitting SQL/Mongo/etc.). Consequences: (1) Location: IEnumerable filters in process; IQueryable filters at the source (WHERE in SQL — less data moved). (2) Translatablity: only provider-supported nodes work (custom C# methods, complex logic throw NotTranslatable — precompute to locals). (3) Timing: both defer; IQueryable executes on enumeration via provider (connection, command, materialization). (4) Composition: queries build incrementally (if (filter) query = query.Where(...)) — one final SQL, no branching queries. (5) AsEnumerable() drops to memory (rest runs client-side — use deliberately for unsupported ops AFTER filtering server-side, never before). (6) AsQueryable() on memory fakes remote (tests!). Expression trees: inspectable code-as-data (used by EF, Moq, serializers); compile with .Compile() to run (used by cached compiled queries). Debugging: ToQueryString() shows SQL; logs show translation warnings (client evaluation = red flag).
internalWorking: Expression<TDelegate> stores the AST (nodes: member access, calls, constants, lambdas). Providers implement IQueryProvider.Execute (walk tree → SQL string + parameters → ADO → materialize). Compiled delegates are JITed machine code. The boundary AsEnumerable just changes the static type (same objects flow).
realWorldUsage: Repository design (return materialized, accept composable IQueryable internally?), dynamic filters, and provider-agnostic data layers.
commonMistake: Custom methods inside IQueryable (runtime translation throw), AsEnumerable before filtering (pulls whole tables!), returning IQueryable from repositories (leaks provider + lifetime + intent), and assuming identical semantics (null handling differs: SQL three-valued vs C# two-valued).
technicalConversation: Ask where their heaviest query filters — SQL WHERE versus in-memory Where after ToList is the single biggest LINQ performance divider.
interviewFollowUp: What is an expression tree, and why can't IQueryable just use compiled delegates?
keyTakeaway: IEnumerable runs code here; IQueryable ships descriptions there. Filter at the source, cross boundaries deliberately.

questionText: What hazards come from enumerating a LINQ query multiple times?
shortAnswer: Re-enumeration re-executes everything: duplicate DB queries, repeated side effects, changed results on mutated sources, and wasted CPU. Materialize once (ToList) when a query is consumed more than once, logged, or crosses a boundary.
detailedAnswer: Each foreach/ToList/Count over a deferred query re-runs the pipeline: two Counts + one ToList = three full passes (three SQL round trips for IQueryable!). Hazards: (1) Performance: N+1-shaped waste invisible in code (query built once, enumerated in a loop). (2) Correctness: source mutated between runs (different answers per run — flaky tests), nondeterministic sources (random/time-based differ), DB data changed between round trips. (3) Side effects multiply (logging predicates, incrementing counters, API calls inside Select — executed per enumeration!). (4) Exceptions repeat or appear late. Diagnostics: query executed once but enumerated K times shows as repeated identical SQL in logs. Fixes: var list = query.ToList() at first multi-use; pass IReadOnlyList into methods (type enforces materialization); repositories return List (never IEnumerable queries); cache expensive predicates' results. Legitimate re-enumeration: cheap pure in-memory pipelines enumerated in different ways (still prefer one materialization for clarity). Analyzer help: some analyzers flag multiple enumeration of the same variable (treat as warnings in hot code).
internalWorking: Each enumeration creates fresh iterators re-pulling the source; IQueryable re-translates (cached plan) + re-executes remotely. No memoization exists in the pipeline by design (queries are descriptions, not results).
realWorldUsage: Count+page pairs, validation-then-process flows, logged queries, and test arrange/act/assert triples over one query.
commonMistake: Count + ToList as separate round trips (standard waste), side-effecting Selects (multiplied effects), and time-varying sources giving inconsistent multi-reads.
technicalConversation: Ask how many SQL statements their list endpoint emits — Count+page is two (correct); Count+page+export-check is three (re-enumeration smell).
interviewFollowUp: How would you design an API so multiple enumeration is impossible by construction?
keyTakeaway: Queries re-run per enumeration. Materialize once at multi-use; return lists, not queries.

questionText: How do closures and loop variables interact with LINQ queries?
shortAnswer: Lambdas capture variables by reference: queries built in a loop over one shared variable all see its final value (for-loops), while foreach gives fresh variables per iteration (C# 5+). Capture copies explicitly when the query outlives the loop.
detailedAnswer: The trap: for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) queries.Add(list.Where(x => x.Id == i)); — all three queries capture the same i, which equals 3 after the loop (all return empty/wrong). foreach (int id in ids) is safe (fresh id per iteration since C# 5). Deferred execution makes it worse: the capture reads at enumeration time (long after the loop), so even 'works in debugger' cases break in production timing. Fixes: copy inside (int current = i; use current), build eagerly (ToList inside the loop), or restructure (ids.SelectMany(id => ...) or Join — no manual loops at all). Same class: captured DbContext/disposables in cached Funcs (lifetime leaks), captured mutable accumulators (race under PLINQ), and modified closures (ReSharper/Rider 'access to modified closure' warnings — heed them). Expression trees capture as constants-ish closures too (EF parameterizes them — loop-built queries get per-iteration parameters, defeating plan caching; build with combined predicates instead).
internalWorking: Closures are compiler classes holding captured variables by reference; all lambdas over the same scope share the instance. for declares one variable for the whole loop; foreach declares per iteration (spec change in C# 5). Deferred queries read the fields when enumerated — arbitrarily later.
realWorldUsage: Dynamic filter builders, loop-generated test cases, partitioned parallel loops, and EF predicate loops.
commonMistake: for-loop captures (the classic), cached delegates over disposables (leaks), and EF loop predicates (parameter explosion — combine with PredicateBuilder/OR instead).
technicalConversation: Ask them to predict the output before running — wrong predictions here are universal, which is why the copy/restructure habit matters more than the rule recitation.
interviewFollowUp: Why did C# 5 change foreach but not for, and what does that tell you about the fix philosophy?
keyTakeaway: Lambdas share loop variables by reference, read at enumeration. Copy inside, or eliminate the loop.

questionText: When should you call ToList, ToArray, ToDictionary, or nothing at all?
shortAnswer: ToList/ToArray when crossing boundaries (return, cache, multi-use, lifetime end), ToDictionary for keyed reuse, nothing when streaming one pass to a terminal op. Each materialization is a full pass + allocation — place it once, at the right boundary.
detailedAnswer: Decision points: (1) Return values: always materialize (List/Array — never queries). (2) Multi-use: one ToList, many reads. (3) Lifetime: DbContext disposal, rented buffers, file handles — materialize before release. (4) Debugging: materialize then inspect (stable snapshot vs shifting query). (5) Caching: store lists, never queries (queries re-run + hold sources). (6) One-shot pipelines ending in foreach/Count/First: no materialization (stream it). ToList vs ToArray: List for further mutation, array for fixed/API shapes (JSON serializes both; arrays slightly leaner). ToDictionary for keyed reuse (dedup first!). ToHashSet for membership reuse. ToLookup for grouped reuse. Async: ToListAsync (single await, streamed server rows). Sizing: ToList over ICollection pre-sizes exactly (no waste); over iterators grows (fine). Over-materialization smell: ToList().Where().ToList().Select().ToList() chains (each an allocation + pass — compose first, materialize once). Under-materialization smell: IEnumerable fields/properties (lifetime + re-run hazards — store lists).
codeExample:
// Compose fully, materialize once:
List<Dto> result = source
    .Where(Predicate)      // deferred
    .Select(Shape)         // deferred
    .OrderBy(Key)          // deferred (buffers on run)
    .Take(50)              // deferred
    .ToList();             // ONE execution, ONE list
internalWorking: ToList enumerates once into a growing buffer (exact-sized when ICollection); ToArray trims to exact; ToDictionary probes per key (duplicate throw). Chained materializations allocate intermediate lists each (GC churn visible in profiles).
realWorldUsage: Repository returns, cached datasets, test fixtures, exported snapshots, and API payloads.
commonMistake: ToList chains (pass+alloc per link), IEnumerable properties (re-run/lifetime traps), and returning arrays from hot paths that callers immediately ToList (pick one).
technicalConversation: Ask them to count materializations in a method — more than one usually means a missing composition step.
interviewFollowUp: Why do repositories return List<T> instead of IEnumerable<T>, even when callers only foreach once?
keyTakeaway: Compose deferred, materialize once at boundaries. Lists for reuse, streams for single passes.

questionText: How do you handle EF Core translation failures and client evaluation warnings?
shortAnswer: Read the exception/log: rewrite with translatable constructs, precompute untranslatable values into locals, or cross AsEnumerable deliberately after server filtering. Never suppress the warning globally — each instance is a correctness/performance decision.
detailedAnswer: Failure shape: InvalidOperationException 'could not be translated' naming the expression — the query dies instead of silently fetching (good default since EF Core 3). Triage: (1) Localize the node (the exception quotes it — often a custom method, DateTime.Now-ish member, or navigation misuse). (2) Precompute: var today = DateTime.UtcNow.Date; ...Where(o => o.Date == today) (locals become parameters). (3) Restructure: split into server part (Where/Select translatable) + AsEnumerable + client part (formatting, complex logic) — AFTER filtering (never before — whole-table pull). (4) Map the untranslatable to SQL: EF.Functions (Like, date parts), value converters, or raw SQL for the fragment (FromSql + compose). Client-eval warnings (where still emitted, e.g. GroupBy tails): treat as errors in review; log them in CI (ConfigureWarnings Throw for RelationalEventId.QueryClientEvaluationWarning in tests!). Testing: ToQueryString assertions on key queries (shape snapshots), translation tests against SQLite/real provider (not just InMemory — it translates nothing), and warning-as-error in the test host. Null semantics: SQL three-valued logic vs C# two-valued (x != null filters differently — know your provider's handling).
internalWorking: The query pipeline binds LINQ nodes to SQL fragments via provider plugins; unbound nodes throw at translation (before any SQL runs — no partial execution). Warnings flow through the EF logging pipeline (event ids) — configurable to throw. Parameters come from captured locals (closure → constant/parameter mapping).
realWorldUsage: Every non-trivial EF query review, provider migrations (SQL Server→Postgres translation deltas), and CI query-shape tests.
commonMistake: Globally suppressing translation warnings (hides table-pulls), AsEnumerable before Where (whole-table fetch), custom helpers inside trees (throw at runtime, not compile time), and testing only against InMemory (translates nothing — false confidence).
technicalConversation: Ask what their CI does about client-evaluation warnings — throw-in-tests is the mature answer; 'we read logs sometimes' is the incident source.
interviewFollowUp: Why is throwing on untranslatable queries better than silently client-evaluating them?
keyTakeaway: Precompute locals, filter server-side, cross to memory deliberately. Warnings are errors in review.

questionText: How do you write custom LINQ operators with extension methods and yield?
shortAnswer: Write static extension methods returning IEnumerable<T> via yield (streaming) with eager argument validation in a wrapper. Follow LINQ conventions: deferred, pure, streaming unless documented, and composable with the standard operators.
detailedAnswer: Shape: public static IEnumerable<T> WhereNotNull<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source) { ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(source); return Core(); static IEnumerable<T> Core() { foreach (T x in source) { if (x is not null) yield return x; } } } — eager validation + deferred core (the framework's own pattern). Conventions: operate on IEnumerable<T> (and IQueryable only if building expression visitors — rare), never mutate inputs, document buffering (a Median operator buffers by nature — say so), name like the domain (Batch/Chunk exists — don't duplicate; DistinctBy covers most). Testing: deferred-ness (no work before enumeration — assert via throwing source), laziness (Take(1) touches minimal input), purity (same input twice → same output), and empty/singleton cases. Async twin: IAsyncEnumerable<T> extensions with CancellationToken ([EnumeratorCancellation]). Reuse: internal 'LinqEx' class per project beats micro-packages; publish only genuinely novel operators. Interop: custom ops compose with EF only after AsEnumerable (they never translate — boundary discipline again).
internalWorking: Same compiler state machines as query operators (nested iterators chain MoveNext). Eager wrapper runs at call; Core defers. No buffering unless the operator demands it (document it when it does).
realWorldUsage: Domain pipelines (active-orders, valid-rows), test-data generators, batching helpers (pre-Chunk), and parsing combinators.
commonMistake: Validation inside the iterator (late throws), buffering silently (document or stream), mutating inputs, and naming collisions with future BCL additions (DistinctBy broke many 'DistinctBy' extensions — namespace carefully).
interviewFollowUp: Why split eager validation from the deferred core instead of validating inside the iterator?
keyTakeaway: Eager-validate, yield-lazily, stay pure and streaming. Conventions make custom ops feel native.

questionText: When should you use PLINQ (AsParallel), and what breaks when you do?
shortAnswer: PLINQ pays off for CPU-bound work over large in-memory sets with independent items (parsing, transforms, searches). It breaks ordering (add AsOrdered), shared-state assumptions (races), and tiny workloads (partition overhead exceeds gains) — and it never applies to EF queries.
detailedAnswer: Use when: CPU-bound per-item cost × large N (image processing, bulk parsing, Monte Carlo), with pure functions over partitioned input. Shape: source.AsParallel().WithDegreeOfParallelism(Environment.ProcessorCount).Where(...).Select(...) — measure: <1ms total workloads slow down (partition + merge overhead). Ordering: lost by default (nondeterministic) — AsOrdered() restores (buffering cost) or order after. Thread-safety: side effects must go (no shared List.Add — use thread-local + merge, locks, or concurrent collections); exceptions aggregate (AggregateException — handle per-item or accept abort). Merge options: WithMergeOptions(ParallelMergeOptions.NotBuffered) for streaming output. EF: AsParallel on IQueryable is meaningless/harmful (queries execute server-side — parallelize across queries with Task.WhenAll instead, minding connection pool limits). Alternatives: Parallel.ForEach(Async) for statement bodies, Channels + workers for pipelines, GPU/vectorize for numeric (SIMD beats threads for simple math). Testing: nondeterministic order tests must sort-then-assert; race tests need stress loops (rarely deterministic — design races out instead).
internalWorking: PLINQ partitions input (range/chunk/hash partitioners), runs the pipeline per partition on pool threads, merges outputs (buffered by default for orderable ops). Shared-state writes race exactly like manual threads — purity is a requirement, not advice.
realWorldUsage: Bulk file parsing, image batch jobs, report crunching, search indexing, and data-migration transforms.
commonMistake: Shared List.Add inside (lost items/corruption — use merge), ordering assumptions (nondeterministic), PLINQ on tiny sets (slower), AsParallel on EF (nonsense — parallelize queries as tasks), and swallowing AggregateException inner details.
technicalConversation: Ask for the measured speedup and core count — sublinear claims without numbers are guesses; 3x on 8 cores for parsing is the typical honest answer.
interviewFollowUp: Why does PLINQ lose ordering, and what does AsOrdered cost you?
keyTakeaway: PLINQ = pure CPU-bound bulk work, measured. Order, state, and tiny sets are its failure modes.

questionText: How do you debug a LINQ pipeline that returns wrong results with no exception?
shortAnswer: Bisect by materializing stages (ToList between links) and comparing counts/samples. Usual culprits: predicate logic (&&/||, nulls), join key mismatch, GroupBy key granularity, premature Take, culture/case comparisons, and client-vs-server null semantics.
detailedAnswer: Method: (1) Materialize each stage into locals and inspect counts + head samples (the 2-minute bisect that finds 90%). (2) Check predicates in isolation (Where clause alone — null propagation? De Morgan slip? case?). (3) Verify keys (join/group keys: watch anonymous-type property names, nulls, case). (4) Check ordering/paging stage (Take before OrderBy? nondeterministic pages?). (5) Compare LINQ-to-Objects vs EF behavior on the same shape (null semantics differ — SQL NULL ≠ C# null in != comparisons!). (6) ToQueryString for the SQL actually emitted (projection surprises, N+1, client-eval). (7) Sample I/O tests: tiny fixed input → expected output per stage (regression-protect the pipeline). Tooling: LINQPad-style dumps, ToQueryString, EF sensitive-data logging in dev (values in SQL — dev only!), and temporary .Select(x => Tap(x)) probes (log-and-pass-through helper, removed after). Prevention: named predicates (testable units), stage-by-stage unit tests with fixed data, and contract tests on comparers/keys.
internalWorking: No magic — wrong results mean wrong logic or wrong data per stage; materialization boundaries make each stage's actual output observable (versus deferred invisibility). SQL-side: parameter sniffing and null semantics are the usual 'same LINQ, different results' sources across providers.
realWorldUsage: Report mismatches, migration validation diffs, feed processing bugs, and flaky data-dependent tests.
commonMistake: Debugging the whole pipeline at once (bisect instead), assuming C# null semantics in SQL (three-valued!), ToString-in-key grouping (culture/case), and leaving Tap probes in production code.
technicalConversation: Ask them to narrate their last wrong-results bug — stage-bisection versus staring is the experience divider.
interviewFollowUp: Give one example where identical LINQ returns different results in memory versus SQL Server.
keyTakeaway: Materialize stages, compare counts, isolate predicates, verify SQL. Bisect, don't stare.
